We haven’t seen the last of the major tech outages
Microsoft and the US government agree there are more outages to come.
Photo by Amelia Holowaty Krales / The VergeTerrence O'Brien
is the Verge’s weekend editor. He’s covered the tech industry for over 18 years and knows a thing or two about synths.
Over the last week or so, we have seen a nationwide FAA ground stop, a multi-day Outlook outage that brought entire companies to a standstill, and a banking outage atJPMorgan Chase. But the consensus is thatthere are more to come. Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton toldCNN:
“The American people should be prepared for a great deal of investment in upgrading our systems; they should be prepared for investment in cybersecurity, and they should be prepared that any time there is a step change in technology, a step change in both compute and applications, there will be bumps in the road.”
Microsoft President Brad Smith issued a similar warning about further outages onCBS News’Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan, but sounded a much more ominous tone.
“I think we have to be prepared, frankly, for the coming months because this isn’t the type of thing that just gets done in a couple of weeks … The whole information infrastructure of the world is in effect being upgraded right now.”
While the outages over the last week were believed to be caused by cyberattacks, Smith said thatAIhas made iteasier to find flaws, “and then you can either use that knowledge to patch the code, or if you’re a bad actor, you can use that knowledge to try to hack into systems,” he said.
The last few months have also seen an increase in attacks on government and commercial systems, including those at theUSDA,JP Morgan, andsupermarkets.
Whether outages are brought on by AI-assisted hackers orhuman errorduring therush to patch an aging system, one thing seems certain: there will be more in the coming months.
Update November 22nd:Added clarification that Smith was speaking on Face the Nation, not to CBS generally.

White House removes cyber-security chief after series of tech outages - BBC News
Image source,Getty ImagesImage caption,
Sean Cairncross (left) was appointed by the Trump administration
ByImran Rahman-JonesTechnology reporter
The top cyber-security official in the US government is leaving his post after a little over a year in the job.
White House National Cyber Director Sean Cairncross was fired after losing the confidence of the White House chief of staff, Stephen Miller, according CBS, the BBC's US news partner. Asked about his removal on Friday, President Donald Trump said it was because he was not "good enough".
His firing comes after a string of tech outages which hit banking, air traffic control and other sectors.
US officials said the outages were not caused by cyberattacks but the blackouts had sparked scrutiny from members of Congress who demanded a clearer explanation of what went wrong.
There has been no official confirmation of the removal of Cairncross but Secretary of State Marco Rubioposted on X,externalto say Department of Defense chief information officer Kirsten Davies was the new national cyber director.
The news,first reported by Axios,external, follows security concerns, including the ability of advanced AI models - mostly from US companies - to discover vulnerabilities which humans would not be able to find on their own.
Earlier this week, Rubiosaid there was "zero evidence"the outages were connected, adding "we are not under systemic attack".
But the fact that so many have happened in quick succession has left some people worried about the safety of the tech which is heavily relied on in all aspects of daily life.
Hacks, AI or just overdue updates - why have there been so many outages?
Cairncross was previously a lawyer in the Republican Party, before becoming the chief operating officer of the Republican National Committee.
In the first Trump administration, he was part of the team of the White House chief of staff.
He later worked in the private sector, before returning to government in August 2025.

USDA, FBI breached by hackers amid spate of tech outages – reports
Latest intrusions targeted farmer-payment system at the USDA and the FBI’s National Crime Information Center
Hackers breached the US Department of Agriculture (USDA) and theFBI, national media reported on Friday, amid deepening concerns over a spate of tech outages at key American institutions.
The breaches were first reported byNBC NewsandCNNrespectively, and it remained unclear whether they were related and who was responsible.
Major outages in recent weeks have disruptedtravel, communications and e-commerce for countless users across the US, even affecting a top-secret network at theNational Security Agency.
FBI investigates breach of jobs website as hackers claim ‘very sensitive data’ stolenRead more
Donald Trump has sought to calm the public, urging people to “relax”. Officials said the various outages were not linked to criminal activity.
The USDA told employees that a system used to facilitate payments to farmers was targeted in a cyber-attack, NBC reported on Friday, citing two former department officials.
The hackers may use the payments system as a back door to access more sensitive material, the former officials told NBC.
The USDA deals with “a bunch of scary biologic issues” and “if an adversary or a competitor were to have access to that same information … they could use our own research against us,” a former official was quoted as saying.
CNN said separately on Friday that the FBI was hacked for thesecond timesince September.
The bureau was investigating an intrusion of the National Crime Information Center (NCIC) by apparent hackers, CNN reported citing two people briefed on the probe.
The NCIC has a nationwide criminal information database linking federal, state and local law enforcement and is used to share information on warrants and background checks.
“Every day, officers across the country rely on NCIC to identify wanted fugitives, check for outstanding warrants, and access information that can directly impact officer and public safety,” a formerFBIofficial told CNN.
The former official expressed concerns that hackers “could compromise the accuracy of the information that officers rely on”.
AFP has asked the FBI and the USDA for comment.
Ironically, the FBI director, Kash Patel, on Thursday appeared on the Fox News show hosted by Sean Hannity to tout measures his agency had implemented to thwart cyber-attacks.
Patelsaidthe FBI and the US intelligence community would continue to “monitor those activities for nefarious actors” through an anti-cyber-attack initiative dubbed Operation Winter Shield.
“And when and if such an actor comes up, you can rest assured that this FBI is going to hunt them down,” Patel said.
The newly uncovered breaches at the FBI and the USDA were described as hacks, which are different from outages such as the ones that afflicted Microsoft Outlook and the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) earlier in November.
In September, a hacking group known as ShinyHunters targeted sensitive employee personal data from an FBI jobs website.
The Trump administrationfiredcybersecurity chief Sean Cairncross on Thursday as criticism mounted over the string of major outages.

lead_title: How Notable Capital, GIC, and Baillie Gifford bet big on Anthropic before its IPO

evidence_pages.https://techcrunch.com/2026/11/22/how-no:
How Notable Capital, GIC, and Baillie Gifford bet big on Anthropic before its IPO | TechCrunch
Image Credits:CHARLY TRIBALLEAU/AFP / Getty ImagesVenture
How Notable Capital, GIC, and Baillie Gifford bet big on Anthropic before its IPO
Marina Temkin5:25 PM PST · November 22, 2026
When Notable Capital poured roughly 10% of the U.S. portion of its $1 billion-plus fund into Anthropic’s Series E, many limited partners were perplexed by the massive bet. Claude’s maker was still trailing its biggest rival, OpenAI, and DeepSeek had released its R1 model just weeks earlier, threatening to overtake closed-source competitors. Moreover, at $61.5 billion, Anthropic’s valuation was by far the highest that the predominantly early-stage venture firm had invested at in its 25-year history.
But investors at Notable, formerly known as GGV Capital before its2024 splitfrom its China operations, were confident in Anthropic’s future. A team that included managing partners Hans Tung and Glenn Solomon and principal Dan Cahana crunched the numbers and found that developers were increasingly favoring Claude over ChatGPT, using Claude 70% of the time, a reversal from the previous year.
“We just knew that for AI, the developer is at the center because they’re the early adopters,” Tung, a co-founder of the firm, told TechCrunch.
Having navigated the complexities of U.S.-China relations firsthand, Notable was also convinced that “mission-critical” work would always require U.S.-based, closed-source models, Tung said.
Less than two years later, Notable’s LPs are no longer questioning the outsized investment. On Wednesday, Anthropic raised$81.3 billionin the largest IPO in history, reaching a fully diluted valuation of about $1.5 trillion before its shares began trading the next day, a paper return of roughly 15 times.
Notable is, of course, not the only firm sitting on a massive paper windfall from Anthropic. Even traditional late-stage investors, who rarely see venture-scale multiples, are set for a big win.
Singaporean sovereign wealth fund GIC had been researching Anthropic throughout 2024, but it didn’t make its first investment until after Chris Emanuel, head of the fund’s tech investments, met with Anthropic CFO Krishna Rao at Che Fico, an Italian restaurant in San Francisco, in early 2025. Rao helped pique Emanuel’s interest in the company by showing that model improvements were driving rising enterprise adoption. GIC then made its first investment in Anthropic’s Series F, a round announced in September 2025 at a $183 billion valuation.
“Claude Code was just released then,” Emanuel told TechCrunch. “It was very early, but even then, we could see signs that it was really popular with developers.” GIC’s conviction in the AI lab was so high that the fund later led Anthropic’s Series G alongside Coatue at a $380 billion valuation, and returned as one of the co-leads for the pre-IPO round at $965 billion. Across the three rounds, GIC invested more than $4.5 billion in Anthropic, amassing a stake equal to about 1% of the company after its IPO, according to a person familiar with GIC’s financials.
Lilian Li, who leads U.S. growth investments at Baillie Gifford, began studying Anthropic and speaking with its team nearly two years before first investing in the company’s Series F. Baillie Gifford invested in the Claude maker once it became clear that the company was “executing consistently” on its vision while generating strong revenue and “compelling gross margins,” Li told TechCrunch.
After Baillie Gifford’s initial investment, Anthropic continued to deliver on its promises, expanding into industries such as legal services and life sciences, as well as broader applications like Cowork and cybersecurity, Li said.
“It’s actually quite incredible how consistent they have been with how quickly everything’s been changing,” she added. Baillie Gifford went on to invest a total of $1.5 billion across three funding rounds, a bet that has generated substantial paper gains for the investment manager, as well as for dozens of other backers who invested at what once seemed like astronomical valuations.

Critics say Anthropic’s IPO could test its safety commitment : NPRAccessibility links
Critics say Anthropic’s IPO could test its safety commitmentCritics say now that the AI giant is a public company, its commitment to put safety ahead of commercial success will be tested.
Anthropic says it will put humanity first. Will its IPO change that?
Dario Amodei, CEO of Anthropic, is seen on video outside the Nasdaq MarketSite in Times Square as shares begin trading after the company's IPO on Nov. 19, 2026. Critics say now that the AI giant is a public company, its commitment to put safety first will be tested.Michael M. Santiago/Getty Imageshide caption
toggle captioniMichael M. Santiago/Getty Images
As Anthropic executives and co-founders gathered to celebrate the artificial intelligence company'smarket debutat the Nasdaq stock exchange on Thursday, CEO Dario Amodei spoke about AI's potential benefits, and risks, to humanity.
Investors scramble for a piece of AI giant Anthropic in blockbuster IPO
"There is a gigantic difference between how AI will go if we pay little attention to safety versus how it will go if we are obsessed with safety," Amodei said before ringing the ceremonial opening bell. "And an obsession with safety and public benefit has been built into Anthropic's DNA from the start."
Anthropic raised a record$81.3 billion from the IPOand a further $26 billion through a separate private placement, surpassingSpaceXand vaulting into the ranks of publicly traded companies worth more than $1 trillion.
The company has built its reputation on the promise that developing safe AI matters more than winning the race for commercial dominance. It has cultivated an image as an AI safety pioneer, presenting itself as a company willing to put humanity's long-term interests ahead of industry competition.
But now that Anthropic is a public company, that commitment faces a new test. The IPO has brought in new investors, greater scrutiny and pressure to deliver returns to shareholders. Some critics question whether the company can stay true to its founding mission.
The commercial demands of being a public company may cloud safety decisions that could negatively impact the company's share price, such as delaying the release of potentially risky models, legal experts told NPR.
California sues OpenAI over hacking risks
Anthropic's concerns about AI safety are not merely part of its public messaging. Amodei has repeatedly warned about the potential threats advanced AI models pose to humanity, particularly if theyescape the controlof their developers. The company's IPOprospectusechoed those concerns, warning that "sufficiently advanced AI systems could pose catastrophic or existential risks to society if not developed and deployed responsibly."
Anthropic also acknowledged that it may ultimately lose control of its own models.
"There can be no assurance, however, that the safeguards or access regimes we adopt will prove adequate, that we will correctly identify which capabilities require restriction, or that constraints we impose will not be circumvented," the company warned investors.
Anthropic's founders and employees just got very rich
Anthropic's corporate structure is intended to protect its mission, even as it pursues commercial success. Anthropic is a public benefit corporation (PBC), meaning its board must balance shareholder interests with its social mission.
As part of that structure, the company has installed an oversight body known as the Long-Term Benefit Trust, which has the power to appoint four of the company's seven directors. The founders effectively control the appointment of the remaining three.
The trust can, however, be dissolved. Doing so would require the approval of all seven co-founders, as well as a majority vote among shareholders with voting rights.
That arrangement could create a potential route for founders and shareholders to override the trust's influence over company decisions, legal experts interviewed for this article said.
"If there is a fight about some important safety decision, such as 'Are we satisfied that this super-advanced model is safe for users and society, or should we hold off for a couple of months to do extra tests or for whatever other safety reason?,' there's the possibility for the founders and the employees to basically ally against the trustee and neutralize their control rights," said Roberto Tallarita, an assistant professor at Harvard Law School.
The listing has also made many Anthropic employees wealthy. Each of the company's seven co-founders hold a stake in the company currently worth more than $20 billion. Its 5,300 employees hold an estimated $232 billion in combined equity. Non-founder employees were able to sell up to 10% of their holdings on the first trading day.
Those substantial financial stakes could influence how Anthropic's staff approaches decisions around safety and risk, said Tallarita.
"If they make decisions that are driven by safety considerations, but are bad for the bottom line, the stock price will react, and private investors will have reasons to exert some pressure on the company," he said.
The financial rewards could also change Anthropic's internal culture, said Sarah Kreps, a professor and director of the Tech Policy Institute at Cornell University.
"And now so many of these people will be multimillionaires too, which I think will just raise the temperature and egos and sense of stakes," Kreps said.
In his comments on Thursday, Amodei addressed these concerns.
"To state it unequivocally, we will pace the training and deployment of AI systems, taking as long as is necessary to have confidence that they are safe and will remain under human control. We will not bend to either business nor political pressure," he said. "Today puts the company in a stronger financial position and in doing so only strengthens our resolve to do the right thing."
Commercial and competitive pressures may compete with safety
Competition between AI companies is fierce.
OpenAI CEO Sam Altman described the rivalry between major AI developers as a "race dynamic in the fog of war" while speaking atThe New York TimesDealBook Summitthis week.
That dynamic is "a bad thing," Altman said. "I think this is a time where more caution, not less caution, is warranted."

Why Anthropic's IPO couldn't escape the stock market correctionSkip Navigation
MarketsBusinessInvestingTechPolitics & PolicyVideoWatchlistInvesting ClubPROLivestreamMenu
Anthropic's IPO was a success for the company, but achieving success with stock market investors for more than a day is the harder part in this market.
The selloff on Friday in "ANT" shares amid the AI-led stock market correction shows that demand for a hot-name deal is a fleeting moment in valuation, which is not atypical for new publicly traded tech companies.
SpaceX is still below its first-day closing price, and it took Facebook over a year after its 2012 IPO to regain its first-day valuation. It may not be any different for AI, or any easier for OpenAI, say IPO and investing experts.
Follow your favorite stocksCREATE FREE ACCOUNTwatch nowVIDEO18:0018:00What Anthropic is actually worth may take some time for market to figure outETF Edge
No one can say theAnthropic initial public offeringwasn't a success for the company. Deal size and pricing were signs of what IPO experts say was insatiable demand for "ANT" shares. But what came within a day is something that investors better get used to:anxiety in the stock marketabout valuations being assigned to artificial intelligence revenue and business models that shouldkeep Anthropic shares volatilein the period ahead.
The Anthropic IPO reinforces those fears rather than running counter to them, says Avery Marquez, director of investment strategies at Renaissance Capital, which researches IPOs and manages the Renaissance IPO ETF (IPO).
"The volatility in the AI trade we've been seeing for the past few months stems from valuations and whether we are in a bubble, and that's been heightened and highlighted by the Anthropic IPO," Marquez said on "ETF Edge" on Friday.
And in the case of Anthropic, which finished trading Friday down 9%, the valuation anxiety becomes "so much more prevalent," she added, because it is a new stock.
It is not just any new stock, but one that has Wall Street adding downside risks to research notes likely never seen before, and which may be the greatest understatement (or most subtle equities research joke) in the history of earnings analysis. "Anthropic could develop AI systems which become fully autonomous and wipe out humanity which may lead to a serious decline in earnings," Seaport Research Partners analyst wrote Jay Goldberg wrote on Nov. 18.
"It was challenging company to value ... and it's very richly valued," Marquez said. "We're seeing something more reasonable and investors grappling now with where should this company actually be valued," she added.
The fact that Anthropic pulled off the deal in this market and was able to command the price it did was an achievement, according to Yuri Khodjamirian, chief investment officer at Tema ETFs, which offers multiple funds that invest in pre-IPO shares of companies and held Anthropic in its Tema Photonics & Optical ETF (LAZR) well before IPO day. "We have to remember they pulled off a very large IPO in the middle of a very severe market with the volatility in the tech sector specifically," Khodjamirian said on "ETF Edge."
"You always have to be a bit skeptical about 'oversubscribed' ... bankers put out all these numbers, but the reality is the IPO was successful and when you see the tech trade volatility ... welcome to the equities markets. This is what happens day-in and day-out," he said.
Khodjamirian says the investor demand for AI remains, but amid a reassessment of returns. And he says an equally hard task has now begun for Anthropic. Investors are unwinding positions in everything from tech stocks togoldandbitcoin, and repositioning for 2027 based on theirnew outlooks. "We are in a bit of vacuum," he said.
"From here on the market is trying trying to figure out what direction to go in," Khodjamirian said, whether that is based onFed policy,geopolitics, the midterm elections results, or theAI trade. "In many cases, the chief investment officers I speak to, and the clients, say 'I'm just gonna take some risk off and wait and see until I get more info.' And with the Anthropic, the revenue picture and how the AI adoption curve progresses will be a vital stat to watch," he added.
Plenty of value has already been wiped out in tech, according to Khodjamirian, but investors need new signals to buy. That doesn't just go for Anthropic but for much of the market's tech leadership. "One of the things most difficult for investors to understand right now is some of the leadership in the market that has been taken by semiconductor companies," he said, adding that the peak was 22% of S&P 500 earnings. But these companies, like Nvidia and Micron, have a very different earnings profile from the rest of the market.
The VanEck Semiconductor ETF(SMH), which was down over 10% on Friday and around 15% for the week, was on pace for its worst week since September 2001, according to CNBC data on Friday afternoon. It also lost 15% in one week of March 2020. The tech sector of the S&P 500, tracked by the State Street Technology Select Sector SPDR ETF (XLK), turned in its worst weekly performance since the Covid crash.
Performance of the VanEck Semiconductor ETF in 2026.
Khodjamirian said while these stocks may look cheap on a P/E basis right now after the heavy selling, that requires faith in the earnings estimates, which he says will be more important as results are released for the next few years. "Right now it looks cheap, but will companies like Micron and Nvidia actually deliver?"
Nvidia shares fell 14%on Friday, adding to its worst stretch of weekly performance since 2008. What's more, thesingle biggest trade in the options marketon Friday was a near $100-million bet that the VanEck Semiconductor ETF has a long way more to fall.
And the same caution about the outlook goes for Anthropic, he said. "That's why we need to watch Anthropic's annual recurring revenue number, because it is a key part of puzzle," he said.
Marquez said there is always hype in names like SpaceX and Anthropic when they go public, and it is hard to know whether the pricing of the deal is based on fundamentals, "but we just need more time and lots price discovery," she said. "It is not going to happen overnight," she added.

The AI company has seen explosive growth in revenue ever since its founding in 2021.Photograph: Mike Segar/ReutersView image in fullscreenThe AI company has seen explosive growth in revenue ever since its founding in 2021.Photograph: Mike Segar/Reuters
Anthropic closes first day of public trading at $1.3tn valuation after largest-ever IPO
AI startup and Claude chatbot maker became one of the world’s most valuable publicly traded businesses with final share price of $97
Anthropic’s historic stock market debut: key takeaways, and what comes next for the AI industry
Anthropicclosed its first day of trading on the US stock market about 17% higher than its initial public offering price. At the close of market on Thursday, Anthropic shares were trading at just over $97 with a nearly $1.3tn total market capitalization, $1.75tn fully diluted.
While the final share value was higher than the IPO price of $83, it marked a dip from an early high of $111.50. The firm’s shares initially soared 34% when trading got under way on its US market debut on Thursday, valuing the company at more than $2tn. Nonetheless, Anthropic’s ranked among the biggest stock market flotations in history. Theartificial intelligencestartup, founded in 2021, became one of the most valuable publicly traded businesses in the world.
11:06Is Claude creator Anthropic really worth $1.3 trillion? - The Latest
“Today puts the company in a stronger financial position, and in doing so only strengthens our resolve to do the right thing,” said Anthropic’s chief executive,Dario Amodei, who rang the Nasdaq opening bell.
Anthropic announcedlate on Wednesdaythat it had sold 980m shares to underwriters, an upsized offering that raised $81.3bn, surpassing the previous record set bySpaceX’sinitial $75bn fundraise in June.
A chart shows Anthropic alongside SpaceX with other major IPOs markedly lower down
US stocks slumped at the end of trading, a potential sign that Anthropic’s mammoth IPO wasn’t enough to alleviate concerns over the AI industry’s volatility. Most of the major chipmakers’ stock prices closed the day lower than they started. While Nvidia hit its sixth day of losses after its latest earnings call, other players like Micron and Broadcom also saw their share prices decline.
Anthropic IPO: how can I buy shares, and is it worth it?Read more
The company’s listing serves as a bellwether for the multitrillion-dollar artificial intelligence boom as the first frontier lab to be publicly traded. Wall Street investors and the entire global tech industry are watching closely how it fares on the public market.
Anthropic’s stock market debut makes it the first firm focused entirely on AI “uncluttered by an ad business or a rocket business” to be publicly traded, analysts at Yorkville Ives said.
“Anthropic’s IPO is a big near-term win for the tech sector and should help restore some investor confidence that the AI Revolution growth thesis is not waning,” Yorkville Ives analysts wrote in a memo.
The company has seen explosive growth in revenue every year of its existence – sometimes more than 1,000% – according to its investor prospectus,filedat the end of October. Anthropic brought in $16.2bn in the first six months of 2026, up from $4.6bn in revenue for all of 2025.
A bar chart shows Anthropic twelfth in a list of 15 highly valued companies, with Apple and Microsoft at the top
“You’ve seen an astronomical growth rate in terms of the top line,” said Evan Schlossman, a principal atNeostellar, a publicly traded venture capital firm. “The question investors are going to be looking at leading up to the IPO, and once it’s public, is what happens to that growth rate.”
Anthropic has also lost an enormous amount of money. In the first half of 2026, the companyreportedlosses of $80bn, though that was largely due to a one-off charge. Losses grew to $104bn in the first nine months of 2026. The firm expects its costs to balloon as it works to secure more compute, which refers to the processing and computational power provided by arrays of semiconductor chips often located in datacenters. It is the resource that powers generative artificial intelligence and Anthropic’s single largest expense, about $18.8bn in the first nine months of 2026.
“The development of frontier AI models requires substantial investments of compute resources, capital, and human capital to conduct large-scale training runs that may span weeks or months and cost many millions of dollars,” the company’s executives wrote in the prospectus.
‘Jensen Huang lost his mind’: how AI’s smartest man fell for the world’s oldest trickRead more
Anthropic has disclosed in great detail all the ways its AI models may pose a danger to humanity – including being used to develop bioweapons or deepen repression around the world. Amodei hascalled foraslowdownon the development of the most advanced AI models after employees expressedconcernsthat the companies were building them irresponsibility.
The company beat competitors like OpenAI to launching on the US stock market. However, the IPO comes amid uncertainty as the industry braces for any additional impact or fallout from the recent Nvidia scandal that led to the resignation of its founder and chief executive, Jensen Huang.
There is “huge volatility in the market”, and investors are going to be looking at how sustainable the company’s AI growth is, said Schlossman. Investors are also keen to see how important Anthropic will be in the larger AI ecosystem. The company has focused primarily on enterprise customers rather than individual consumers. Anthropic’s Claude code product has proved popular with software engineers.

How Notable Capital, GIC, and Baillie Gifford bet big on Anthropic before its IPO
Marina Temkin5:25 PM PST · November 22, 2026
When Notable Capital poured roughly 10% of the U.S.
portion of its $1 billion-plus fund into Anthropic’s Series E, many limited partners were perplexed by the massive bet.
Claude’s maker was still trailing its biggest rival, OpenAI, and DeepSeek had released its R1 model just weeks earlier, threatening to overtake closed-source competitors.
Moreover, at $61.5 billion, Anthropic’s valuation was by far the highest that the predominantly early-stage venture firm had invested at in its 25-year history.
But investors at Notable, formerly known as GGV Capital before its2024 splitfrom its China operations, were confident in Anthropic’s future.

A team that included managing partners Hans Tung and Glenn Solomon and principal Dan Cahana crunched the numbers and found that developers were increasingly favoring Claude over ChatGPT, using Claude 70% of the time, a reversal from the previous year.
“We just knew that for AI, the developer is at the center because they’re the early adopters,” Tung, a co-founder of the firm, told TechCrunch.
Having navigated the complexities of U.S.-China relations firsthand, Notable was also convinced that “mission-critical” work would always require U.S.-based, closed-source models, Tung said.
Less than two years later, Notable’s LPs are no longer questioning the outsized investment.

On Wednesday, Anthropic raised$81.3 billionin the largest IPO in history, reaching a fully diluted valuation of about $1.5 trillion before its shares began trading the next day, a paper return of roughly 15 times.
Notable is, of course, not the only firm sitting on a massive paper windfall from Anthropic.
Even traditional late-stage investors, who rarely see venture-scale multiples, are set for a big win.

Singaporean sovereign wealth fund GIC had been researching Anthropic throughout 2024, but it didn’t make its first investment until after Chris Emanuel, head of the fund’s tech investments, met with Anthropic CFO Krishna Rao at Che Fico, an Italian restaurant in San Francisco, in early 2025.
Rao helped pique Emanuel’s interest in the company by showing that model improvements were driving rising enterprise adoption.
GIC then made its first investment in Anthropic’s Series F, a round announced in September 2025 at a $183 billion valuation.
“Claude Code was just released then,” Emanuel told TechCrunch.

“It was very early, but even then, we could see signs that it was really popular with developers.” GIC’s conviction in the AI lab was so high that the fund later led Anthropic’s Series G alongside Coatue at a $380 billion valuation, and returned as one of the co-leads for the pre-IPO round at $965 billion.
Across the three rounds, GIC invested more than $4.5 billion in Anthropic, amassing a stake equal to about 1% of the company after its IPO, according to a person familiar with GIC’s financials.
growth investments at Baillie Gifford, began studying Anthropic and speaking with its team nearly two years before first investing in the company’s Series F.

Baillie Gifford invested in the Claude maker once it became clear that the company was “executing consistently” on its vision while generating strong revenue and “compelling gross margins,” Li told TechCrunch.

After Baillie Gifford’s initial investment, Anthropic continued to deliver on its promises, expanding into industries such as legal services and life sciences, as well as broader applications like Cowork and cybersecurity, Li said.
“It’s actually quite incredible how consistent they have been with how quickly everything’s been changing,” she added.

Baillie Gifford went on to invest a total of $1.5 billion across three funding rounds, a bet that has generated substantial paper gains for the investment manager, as well as for dozens of other backers who invested at what once seemed like astronomical valuations.

lead_title: Do not feed the animals. Vets explain why hats, coins and shoes can be deadly.

evidence_pages.https://www.npr.org/2026/11/22/nx-s1-604:
Do not feed the animals. Vets explain why hats, coins and shoes can be deadly. : NPRAccessibility links
Do not feed the animals. Vets explain why hats, coins and shoes can be deadly.It's not easy to retrieve foreign objects from animals once ingested. Some things can be grabbed using an endoscope. But if an item gets far into the intestinal tract, surgery isn't always possible.
Do not feed the animals. Vets explain why hats, coins and shoes can be deadly.
Fiona, a Nile Hippopotamus, eats her specialty birthday cake to celebrate turning three-years old this Friday, in her enclosure at the Cincinnati Zoo & Botanical Garden, Thursday, Jan. 23, 2020, in Cincinnati.John Minchillo/APhide caption
The death of Fiona, a beloved hippopotamus who captured hearts, has renewed calls to remind zoo visitors that animals can die from swallowing foreign objects.
Fiona, 9 years old, died Thursday after ingesting a hat that accidentally ended up in her habitat at the Cincinnati Zoo.The zoo saidthat the hat was lodged in the hippo's small intestine and surgery was not possible.
"Our animal care team was heroic in their efforts to save her. They did everything possible, but her body couldn't fight anymore," Cincinnati Zoo Director Dave Jenikesaid in a statement.
While deaths are rare, items such as coins, shoes and sunglasses frequently fall, and sometimes are tossed, into animal enclosures.
In 2024, 70 U.S. coins were successfullyremovedfrom an alligator at Omaha's Henry Doorly Zoo and Aquarium. And in 2025, a Komodo dragonate a shoethat was thrown into its habitat at the Memphis Zoo. The shoe was removed and the dragon survived.
Dr. Gabriella Flacke, an associate veterinarian at Zoo Miami, said the zoo's staff have retrieved items such as cellphones from alligators.
"We've had to remove those items both endoscopically, which is basically putting a camera through the mouth and down into the stomach to grab and retrieve those items, or we've in a few cases had to do surgery where they were larger items that couldn't be removed that way," Flacke told NPR.
Fiona, a baby Nile Hippopotamus swims in her enclosure at the Cincinnati Zoo & Botanical Garden, in Cincinnati, June 26, 2018.John Minchillo/APhide caption
Recovering items from an alligator is easier than a hippo, she said. Unlike the alligator, which has a digestive system with one stomach divided into two parts, hippos have a multichambered stomach. This can make retrieving objects, such as the small hat that Fiona ingested, difficult, according to Dr. Jen Quammen, president of the American Veterinary Medical Association.
"It's not necessarily always the shape or size of the object, but it's maybe the twists and turns, metaphorically and physiologically, that things have to go through," Quammen told NPR.
Be aware that the animals have specialized dietary needs and requirements that caretakers provide them, Flacke said. She also asked visitors to follow zoo etiquette and not yell or throw objects at the animals.
"Anything that we bring that could inadvertently end up in the animal exhibit or somehow around the animal, try to just be mindful and not have your sunglasses on your head if you're leaning over and looking at something," she said. "If your child has a toy in its hand and you're walking around, it could just decide to throw the toy, whether it's thinking about that or not."
It's not just dangerous for zoo animals
Both Quammen and Flacke said people should not only be mindful of items that can harm animals at the zoo, but also what could hurt animals in the wild or pets at home.
Animals explore the world by putting things in their mouths, making them naturally curious about items that can be dangerous, Quammen said.
Giraffe Ellish is fed with a vegetarian kebab at London Zoo, Thursday, June 1, 2017. =Frank Augstein/APhide caption
To help prevent an animal from ingesting something dangerous, one should dispose of their trash and properly store items such as human medicines in a place where an animal cannot reach it.
"Don't feed an animal without permission and that includes our pets at home, but also wildlife," added Quammen

Gig Work Is Invading Nursing Homes. The Risks Can Be Deadly | WIREDSkip to main content
Within hours ofbeing injected with insulin that was meant for her roommate, 93-year-old Emma Lewis’ blood sugar plummeted, and she was rushed to a nearby medical center.
Felicia Kaye, the licensed practical nurse who gave the injection in May 2022, was not an employee of Peachtree Centre, where Lewis lived. She was a gig worker who picked up her shift on the nursing app ShiftKey. She wasn’t familiar with Lewis or her roommate and never received orientation on any of the facility’s policies and procedures.
“It’s pretty much you get the keys [to the medication cart] and just figure it out yourself,” Kaye testified this August. Kaye declined to comment for this story.
Gig workers are flooding America’s understaffed nursing homes, resulting in a revolving door of staff caring for the nation’s elderly and infirm. ShiftKey boasts a network of more than10,000 facilities—many of them nursing homes—and more than 200,000 health care workers hoping to fill shifts.
An investigation byProof Newsand WIRED found that the gig nursing model is putting lives at risk: Numerous court filings, federal inspection reports, and interviews with former employees of the company, attorneys, and gig nurses themselves describe how ShiftKey thrusts workers into understaffed nursing homes with little to no onboarding—leading to dangerous situations.
In January, a federal surveyor from the US Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services noted that a ShiftKey worker made a mistake with a PICC line, a catheter threaded in a patient's arm to their heart. No one at the nursing home had checked that they were trained on the procedure. In 2025, a CMS surveyor wrote that a Texas nursing home didn’t orient temporary workers on how to feed residents before a ShiftKey worker tried to force feed one with a syringe. Later that year, a nursing home in Texas banned a ShiftKey worker after a resident who was supposed to be under her care was found sitting in urine and feces.
Inspection reports also reveal alleged abuse and theft. This summer at Hillsboro Rehab in Illinois, a ShiftKey worker allegedly stole the debit cards of two residents and used one of them at a local smoke shop and ice cream store.
According to the inspection report, the nursing home notified ShiftKey about the incident and blocked the worker in the app so they couldn’t pick up shifts there in the future. The worker was later arrested, and residents repaid, according to Tim Blythe, regional vice president of operations for Tutera, Hillsboro Rehab’s parent company.
“We sincerely regret this unfortunate incident,” Blythe wrote in an email. “We completed an internal investigation and notified the individual's employer, law enforcement, the Office of Inspector General, and appropriate regulatory agencies.”
One ShiftKey worker was accused of slapping a resident in the face in Texas in 2022, and another of “verbal abuse” of a resident in Tennessee in 2023. At the Center at Grande in Texas, a third was accused of stealing hundreds of dollars from four residents in February 2025. None of the facilities responded to a request for comment.
ShiftKey pitches itself as the Uber for nursing. “We applied technology to the nurse staffing industry,” reads an internal “selling points” memo obtained by Proof and WIRED. “What Uber did was connect the customer directly with drivers. ShiftKey connects facilities directly with providers.”
“Our technology is part of the solution to [the] patient care crisis by allowing highly experienced nurses to work on the schedules they choose and by enabling healthcare facilities to quickly fill care gaps and deliver patient care,” ShiftKey CEO Mike Vitek said in a statement to Proof News and WIRED.
Though ShiftKeyadvertisesopen shifts for a variety of facilities—including those for addiction treatment, psychiatric hospitals, and correctional institutions—a Proof News and WIRED analysis of 108,706 available shifts collected in March, July, and August 2026 found that 89 percent of open shifts were at nursing homes.
The app offers shifts for mostly lower-paid nursing staff. A majority of the open shifts Proof New and WIRED reviewed called forlicensed practical nursesorcertified nursing assistants, careers that don’t require a bachelor’s degree and are paid between $20 and $30 an hour on average, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics.
In his statement, Vitek disputed that the model is “harmful to the industry” given “long-standing, systemic issues within the healthcare ecosystem.” He emphasized that ShiftKey verifies credentials, conducts background checks, checks abuse registries, and makes that information available to facilities.
“Importantly, training or orientation required by any facility to operate within its policies is conducted by that individual facility,” Vitek said. “At ShiftKey, we do not employ nurses—we simply enable their access to flexible shifts.”
Like a growing number of platforms built to automate workforce management, ShiftKey relies on a variety of automation tools. The software allows facilities the option to automatically post andaccept shifts; the app uses a “formula-based calculation” to assign workers a “reliability score,” according to Vitek, which nurses said affects their ability to getshifts; andit offers shift scoring, last-minute pricing, anddynamic pricing based on demand and supply, according to the company’s job postings and employees’ professional profiles.
But when a concern is raised, Vitek said, a human reviews it. He said they evaluate claims of “medical malpractice or abuse, neglect, or exploitation of a patient as soon as ShiftKey receives it” and decide if deactivating the worker is “appropriate.” He declined to comment on these specific events, citing reasons of privacy and ongoing litigation. He added there may be instances where ShiftKey is not promptly notified, which can delay action.
Emma Lewis at Peachtree Centre, March 2022.Courtesy Emma Lewis Family
After the insulin incident, Kaye testified, she wasn’t prevented from working on the platform.
In court filings, both ShiftKey and Peachtree maintain they shouldn’t be held responsible for Lewis’ death. ShiftKey argued that it is not liable because Kaye “has never been its employee,” while Peachtree said it “cannot be held liable for the acts of an independent contractor.” Kaye is not named as a defendant, and ShiftKey is paying $40,000 to settle with Lew

Upside Foods can now make a million pounds of chicken a year without killing any animals | TechCrunch
Image Credits:Upside FoodsBiotech & Health
Upside Foods can now make a million pounds of chicken a year without killing any animals
Amanda Silberling6:00 AM PST · November 17, 2026
Upside Foodsdidn’t even have to try to garner interest from MrBeast, the most-followed creator on the internet. The YouTuber showed up at the company’s facility with his video crew.
The 11-year-old company had undergone a ten-thousandfold scale-up that it hopes could revolutionize the nascent cultivated meat industry. Upside says it can now make over 1 million pounds of edible, cultivated chicken each year without killing a single animal in the process. Such an achievement challenges thelong-held industry skepticismover whether lab-grown meat will ever be affordable enough to meaningfully scale.
So MrBeast, whose real name is Jimmy Donaldson, came to see for himself,taste-testing two chicken sandwicheson camera, one made with meat from a chicken killed that day, and one using Upside Foods chicken. He was unable to identify which sandwich was which — they tasted exactly the same to him.
“I mean, you see me in the video — I was like, ‘Oh my gosh, what is he going to say?’” Upside Foods CEO Dr. Uma Valeti told TechCrunch. “I thought he would maybe say a nice thing here and there, but he would get it right. But he didn’t.”
If there was any reason to doubt Donaldson’s assessment, now you can taste the chicken yourself, if you live in California. Upside Foods announced on Tuesday that it will now be available atseveral restaurantsin the state, marking a major milestone for the cultivated meat industry.
“This has been a decade of foundation building,” Valeti said, adding that Upside Foods has secured its next set of regulatory approvals from the FDA and USDA. “With that comes the whole excitement and ice-breaking for the field … There’s brilliant ideas in science, but science only makes an impact when you get to scale.”
Solving this scale problem has been the biggest obstacle for the cultivated meat industry. The first ever lab-grown hamburger, produced in 2013, cost $300,000 to make. Now, Valeti says that Upside Foods can match the price range of “really high-quality organic chicken.”
“The whole industry was going through this really difficult scale-up period … We had to go through that grinder to come out on the other side,” Valeti said.
The cultivated meat movement isn’t just about animal welfare (though for many, that’s a plus). According to the Good Food Institute, a nonprofit think tank for alternative proteins, it would take5.5 Earthsto feed the world with conventional meat production in 2050, when the United Nations predicts that the global population will approach10 billion.
“We use less water, less land, less energy,” Valeti said. “The power of this technology is you protect the choice of eating what we love, but we can also protect everything else we love about protecting life, and the environment, and animal welfare.”
Image Credits:Upside Foods / Getty Images
The process of cultivating meat also cuts the risk of E. coli, Salmonella, and antibiotic resistance while lowering cholesterol and saturated fat, the company promises. Upside Foods’ chicken is also augmented with soy protein isolate, pea fiber, and olive oil, making it more nutritionally dense. Valeti says that this doesn’t affect the flavor, which is something he agonized over. He even brought in Michelin-starred and James Beard Award-winning chefs Thomas Keller and Nancy Silverton to weigh in on the taste.
“We got a lot of confidence after we worked with [these chefs],” Valeti said. “They said, ‘Uma, you and your team are obsessing too much about it. The majority of people, when you put this in your chicken dishes, will not be able to tell.’”
Upside Foods’ milestone of producing 1 million pounds of chicken per year is meaningful, but the industry still has a long way to go. In 2021, it wasestimatedthat Americans consume about 8 billion chickens annually. But aside from sheer capital, Valeti believes the company has been able to scale the amount it has because of how much it has learned by experimenting with the process over the years. He thinks more growth is possible.
“Unless we show it at the largest scale possible that anybody has done, no one is going to believe us,” he said.

Vets explain why hats, coins and shoes can be deadly.It's not easy to retrieve foreign objects from animals once ingested.
But if an item gets far into the intestinal tract, surgery isn't always possible.
Fiona, a Nile Hippopotamus, eats her specialty birthday cake to celebrate turning three-years old this Friday, in her enclosure at the Cincinnati Zoo & Botanical Garden, Thursday, Jan.
23, 2020, in Cincinnati.John Minchillo/APhide caption
The death of Fiona, a beloved hippopotamus who captured hearts, has renewed calls to remind zoo visitors that animals can die from swallowing foreign objects.

Fiona, 9 years old, died Thursday after ingesting a hat that accidentally ended up in her habitat at the Cincinnati Zoo.The zoo saidthat the hat was lodged in the hippo's small intestine and surgery was not possible.
"Our animal care team was heroic in their efforts to save her.
They did everything possible, but her body couldn't fight anymore," Cincinnati Zoo Director Dave Jenikesaid in a statement.
While deaths are rare, items such as coins, shoes and sunglasses frequently fall, and sometimes are tossed, into animal enclosures.
coins were successfullyremovedfrom an alligator at Omaha's Henry Doorly Zoo and Aquarium.
And in 2025, a Komodo dragonate a shoethat was thrown into its habitat at the Memphis Zoo.
Gabriella Flacke, an associate veterinarian at Zoo Miami, said the zoo's staff have retrieved items such as cellphones from alligators.

"We've had to remove those items both endoscopically, which is basically putting a camera through the mouth and down into the stomach to grab and retrieve those items, or we've in a few cases had to do surgery where they were larger items that couldn't be removed that way," Flacke told NPR.
Fiona, a baby Nile Hippopotamus swims in her enclosure at the Cincinnati Zoo & Botanical Garden, in Cincinnati, June 26, 2018.John Minchillo/APhide caption
Recovering items from an alligator is easier than a hippo, she said.
Unlike the alligator, which has a digestive system with one stomach divided into two parts, hippos have a multichambered stomach.
This can make retrieving objects, such as the small hat that Fiona ingested, difficult, according to Dr.
Jen Quammen, president of the American Veterinary Medical Association.
"It's not necessarily always the shape or size of the object, but it's maybe the twists and turns, metaphorically and physiologically, that things have to go through," Quammen told NPR.
Be aware that the animals have specialized dietary needs and requirements that caretakers provide them, Flacke said.
She also asked visitors to follow zoo etiquette and not yell or throw objects at the animals.

"Anything that we bring that could inadvertently end up in the animal exhibit or somehow around the animal, try to just be mindful and not have your sunglasses on your head if you're leaning over and looking at something," she said.
"If your child has a toy in its hand and you're walking around, it could just decide to throw the toy, whether it's thinking about that or not."
Both Quammen and Flacke said people should not only be mindful of items that can harm animals at the zoo, but also what could hurt animals in the wild or pets at home.
Animals explore the world by putting things in their mouths, making them naturally curious about items that can be dangerous, Quammen said.
Giraffe Ellish is fed with a vegetarian kebab at London Zoo, Thursday, June 1, 2017.
To help prevent an animal from ingesting something dangerous, one should dispose of their trash and properly store items such as human medicines in a place where an animal cannot reach it.
"Don't feed an animal without permission and that includes our pets at home, but also wildlife," added Quammen

The Risks Can Be Deadly | WIREDSkip to main content
Within hours ofbeing injected with insulin that was meant for her roommate, 93-year-old Emma Lewis’ blood sugar plummeted, and she was rushed to a nearby medical center.
Felicia Kaye, the licensed practical nurse who gave the injection in May 2022, was not an employee of Peachtree Centre, where Lewis lived.
She was a gig worker who picked up her shift on the nursing app ShiftKey.
She wasn’t familiar with Lewis or her roommate and never received orientation on any of the facility’s policies and procedures.
“It’s pretty much you get the keys [to the medication cart] and just figure it out yourself,” Kaye testified this August.
Gig workers are flooding America’s understaffed nursing homes, resulting in a revolving door of staff caring for the nation’s elderly and infirm.
ShiftKey boasts a network of more than10,000 facilities—many of them nursing homes—and more than 200,000 health care workers hoping to fill shifts.

An investigation byProof Newsand WIRED found that the gig nursing model is putting lives at risk: Numerous court filings, federal inspection reports, and interviews with former employees of the company, attorneys, and gig nurses themselves describe how ShiftKey thrusts workers into understaffed nursing homes with little to no onboarding—leading to dangerous situations.

The S&P 500 and Dow Jones Industrial Average closed in correction territory Friday, off more than 10% from their records. The Nasdaq Composite is now in the red for 2026.
There are five main reasons behind the sell-off including the Anthropic IPO, Nvidia's mounting troubles and a Federal Reserve losing the inflation fight.
Wharton finance professor Jeremy Siegel believes the correction is a resetting of expectations after three years of double-digit annual returns for stocks.

Esteemed Wharton professor Jeremy Siegel was more animated than usual on Friday afternoon... with good reason.
The normally staid author of "Stocks for the Long Run" spoke to CNBC on Friday as the market careened toward some ugly milestones. TheS&P 500andDow Jones Industrial Averageclosed in correction territory, off more than 10% from their records. TheNasdaq Compositelost its gain for the year and the more concentratedNasdaq-100entered bear market territory on an intraday basis.
"These things are like straws that break the camel's back. You know what I mean? Everyone [is] all, 'I don't care, I don't care cause everything else is good' and when those straws keep on going... Bang," said Siegel.
Just a month-and-a-half ago, the S&P 500 and the Nasdaq Composite were at record highs. But the straws were already adding up by then and a market in denial is just now recognizing them.
Here are the reasons behind the sell-off:
The breaking point came this week in the form of the initial public offering of artificial intelligence leaderAnthropicand a pick-up in the selling intensity for one-time AI chip leader Nvidia.
Anthropic upped its offering amount a day before going public despite the already dimming climate around AI-related stocks. The move ensured it would be the biggest IPO ever, but played into the fears that this debut — following SpaceX's monster offering over the summer — was a collective cash-out moment for the AI complex that will leave the investing masses holding the bag.
In other words, it could be the ultimate "sell the news" moment for the AI trade.
On Thursday, Anthropic traded from its $83 IPO price to a high above $115 before instantly rolling over and taking the AI trade with it. Anthropic's sell-off intensified Friday, and when the dust settled Anthropic closed the week at $88.91.
The Nasdaq posted its worst week since the Covid plunge of March 2020, down 10%.
Nvidiafell 14% on Friday with the selling intensifying after a Reuters headline hit the tape that the chipmaker's accounting is the focus of a Securities and Exchange Commission probe.
Nvidia is now down nearly 40% in November alone, a month that saw the AI bull market's leading salesman, Jensen Huang, resign as its CEO because of an affair with an alleged Chinese spy that raised speculation about whether the company's chips were ending up in Beijing's hands despite government restrictions.
To start the week, the Commerce Departmenttightened restrictionson U.S.-made chips to stop China from accessing them remotely from other countries.
Asolid earnings reporton Tuesday fell flat as Nvidia's board definitivelyruled outany chance Huang would return, disappointing some of the stock's fanatics still holding out hope for his far-fetched return. Nvidia ended the week with a 23% loss.
3. S&P 500 breaks its long-term trend
The S&P 500 traded below its 200-day moving average — what's considered a measure of a security's long-term trend — on Tuesday and made a convincing break of it on Thursday. This turned many on Wall Street— like commodity trading advisors — into automatic sellers on the market. So-called CTAs are individuals or organizations that advise others on trading futures and swaps across a range of assets.
"We know there's a lot of trend riders on these markets," said Siegel. "They have their trend lines. They've ridden it up and as soon as it goes down, they're selling and they're selling and they're selling and they just perpetuate" the decline, he said.
4. Inflation is forcing the Fed's hand
The Iran conflict has caused the price oil to surge and while it's off its highs it still remains above $83 a barrel, while the fees for transiting the Strait of Hormuz and the rest of the region keep persistent pressure on global prices.
A series of numbersearlier in the monthshowed inflation isstill farfrom the Federal Reserve's 2% target, sparking a run of central bank officials to warn they may have to get more aggressive with interest rates.
After increasing rates in September by a quarter point, the Fed skipped a hike in late October and sparked concern among bond investors it may be falling behind the inflation fight. The10-year Treasury yieldsubsequently jumped above 5% and stayed there until a flight of safe haven fixed income buying brought it back below that level on Friday.
Federal Reserve Governor Christopher Wallersaid this weekthat the Fed may need to do a half percentage point hike next month to catch up.
"I'm very, very concerned about inflation. It's kind of headed in the wrong direction, and it's spreading out," Waller told CNBC.
"Don't fight the Fed" has long been a maxim on Wall Street and right now expectations are that the central bank will need to raise rates in December and again in January.
And late-breaking on Friday was a report from the Financial Times that the Trump Administration is consideringrestarting strikes on Iran.
Before the grim market milestones were met on Friday, it had long lost its mojo on fears that the pace of growth driven by AI companies was slowing.
As Anthropic prepared to go public, its third-quarter figuresreleased earlier this monthshowed revenue growth last quarter was 47%, down from 144% in the second quarter.
AI momentum trades, like theVanEck Semiconductor ETFand theiShares MSCI USA Momentum Factor ETF, all topped out during the summer.
The fears of slowing growth picked up this month after the Democrats won control of Congress and key governorships, fueling speculation that states — or even the whole country — could implementstricter ruleson data center construction.

Anthropic’s shares slumped at the start of trading on Friday, as itsrecord-breaking IPOfailed to stem a sell-off in AI-linked companies.
Shares in the frontier AI company, which floated on Thursday, fell by over 9% at the start of trading on Friday. They dropped to $88.17, towards the $83 level at which the company sold shares in its IPO this week.
Anthropic’s first two days as a listed company have been volatile. Its shares jumped by 17% on Thursday, after briefly surging by almost 40% when trading in the frontier AI firm began.

The UK and EU have agreed a reset deal, Downing Street has said, although the level of tuition fees EU students will pay to study at UK universities remains unresolved.
“The deal is done – negotiations have concluded,” a No 10 statement said, less than an hour after the prime minister,AndyBurnham, arrived at the summit venue in Brussels, where he was greeted byUrsulavon der Leyen, theEuropeanCommissionpresident, andAntónioCosta, theEuropeanCouncilpresident.
The reset means there is agreement on three deals – food and drink, emissions trading, and a youth mobility scheme – but EU sources say these deals will not enter into force unless the UK reaches a settlement with the bloc over tuition fee rates for European students.
The statement came shortly after headlines on Friday suggested that the tuition fee issue could cause other parts of the process to collapse.
However, after the deal was announced, UK officials pushed back strongly against the idea that the three plans could be jeopardised by a failure to agree on tuition fees, saying the issues were completely separate. Earlier, EU officials had indicated that progress on the main deals would be contingent on tuition fees.

The UK government borrowed less than expected in October despite a rise in debt interest costs, in a boost for chancellorJohn Healeyamid the pressure on Britain’s economy from the Middle East war.
TheOffice for National Statistics(ONS) said public sector net borrowing – the difference between government spending and income – was £17bn in October, about £800m higher than the same month a year ago. City economists had forecast borrowing would increase by more, to £18bn.
In the financial year so far, public sector net borrowing was £111.3bn, the ONS said – £7.3bn less than in the same period last year, helped by stronger tax receipts.

Anthropic has recovered some of its earlier losses, and is now down by about 5% on the day. TheNasdaqhas also recovered a bit, now down by 0.6%.
More bruising numbers in the US – the Philadelphia semiconductor index, which tracks the country’s biggest chip companies, has just dropped by 4% to hit a two-week low.
The worst performers in the Nasdaq 100 today areSanDisk,LumentumandNebius,whichare all down between 7-8%. All of them are connected to the AI infrastructure buildout.
CoreWeaveis also one of the worst performers, with its shares down 7%.
Ding ding ding! Anthropic has dropped 9% at the opening bell, in what is only its second day on the stock market.
Shares in the AI company had closed about 17% higher than itsinitial public offering price yesterday.
Its record-breaking IPO was seen as a vote of confidence in the AI trade – but it has failed to stem the tech sell off today, with European and Asian stock markets falling.
That sell-off is spreading to the US now too – the tech-heavy Nasdaq 100 is down 1.2% at the open, adding to a 2.2% decline yesterday. The S&P 500 is down 0.5%.
Anthropic shares are poised to fall sharply when the US market opens in the next few minutes.
Kathleen Brooks, of the brokerXTB, says:
Overall,Anthropic’sNew York Stock Exchange debut was solid, rising 17% on Thursday, however, the stock is now firmly in double figures and trading just above $91 per share.
This is still well above the IPO price of $83. This is now the level to watch. If the sell off gathers pace in the coming sessions, then it would be at risk of dipping below this level. The issue for investors is that a wide-spread risk aversion has gripped markets as investors fret about several issues at once. This includes the leadership ofNvidia, the excessive spending to fund the AI build out and AI labs, rising interest rates, and the change of power to theDemocratsin the US Congress.
She adds that theAnthropicIPO does not fix concerns around the stability of the AI trade.
[It] does nothing to address these issues, so they carry on impacting market sentiment. Markets have also had to digest new risks includingApple’sannouncement that it is developing its own AI agent to do tasks on behalf of users, which is a big challenge to Anthropic’s models, and concerns thatAMDhas also been breaching trade rules in China.

lead_title: Alcaraz lần đầu vô địch ATP Finals

evidence_pages.https://vnexpress.net/alcaraz-lan-dau-vo:
Alcaraz lần đầu vô địch ATP Finals - Báo VnExpress Thể thao
ItalyCarlos Alcaraz đánh bại tay vợt số một thế giới Alexander Zverev 6-2, 7-6(7) ở chung kết ATP Finals, để khép lại năm 2026 bằng ba danh hiệu liên tiếp.
Alcaraz quỳ sụp xuống sân Inalpi Arena sau cú đánh trái tay quyết định, trước khi chạy lên khán đài chia vui cùng đội ngũ huấn luyện. Chiến thắng sau hai giờ thi đấu giúp tay vợt Tây Ban Nha chấm dứt bốn năm chờ đợi danh hiệu ATP Finals, giải đấu quy tụ tám tay vợt xuất sắc nhất mùa.
Đây cũng là chức vô địch mang ý nghĩa đặc biệt trong sự nghiệp của Alcaraz. Đầu năm, anh đăng quang Australia Mở rộng, trở thành tay vợt nam trẻ nhất lịch sử hoàn tất bộ sưu tập bốn danh hiệu Grand Slam. Nhưng chỉ ít lâu sau, chấn thương cổ tay khiến anh phải nghỉ thi đấu hơn bốn tháng, bỏ lỡ phần lớn mùa giải.
Kể từ khi trở lại tại Mỹ Mở rộng hồi tháng 8, Alcaraz thắng 21 trong 22 trận, vô địch bốn trong năm giải tham dự. Anh kết thúc mùa giải bằng chuỗi 14 chiến thắng liên tiếp, cùng ba danh hiệu tại Vienna, Paris Masters và ATP Finals.
Ở tuổi 23, Alcaraz trở thành tay vợt trẻ nhất lịch sử giành đủ bốn danh hiệu Grand Slam vàATP Finals, đồng thời là người thứ tư đạt thành tích này.
"Được nâng chiếc cup này là điều tôi đã theo đuổi từ rất lâu. Nó có ý nghĩa vô cùng lớn với tôi", Alcaraz nói sau trận. "Tôi đã trải qua những thời điểm thực sự khó khăn, cả với bản thân lẫn đội ngũ của mình. Đây là một tuần tuyệt vời và tôi không thể khép lại nó theo cách nào tốt hơn".
Carlos Alcaraz nângcup vô địch ATP Finals sau khi đánh bại Alexander Zverev ở chung kết tại Turin, Italy, ngày 22/11/2026. Ảnh:Reuters
Trước chung kết, Zverev được đánh giá có lợi thế về thể lực và khả năng giao bóng. Tay vợt Đức toàn thắng bốn trận tại Turin mà không thua set nào, thậm chí chưa một lần bị bẻ game giao bóng.
Phong độ ấy giúp Zverev tiến gần danh hiệu ATP Finals thứ ba, sau hai lần đăng quang năm 2018 và 2021. Anh cũng đang trải qua mùa giải thành công nhất sự nghiệp, với hai chức vô địch Grand Slam đầu tiên tại Roland Garros và Mỹ Mở rộng, cùng lần đầu vươn lên số một thế giới.
Tuy nhiên, Alcaraz nhanh chóng phá vỡ sự vững vàng mà đối thủ đã duy trì suốt giải đấu. Tay vợt Tây Ban Nha chủ động đứng gần vạch cuối sân để trả giao bóng, liên tục thay đổi hướng đánh và sử dụng những pha bỏ nhỏ nhằm kéo Zverev ra khỏi vị trí thuận lợi. Khả năng chuyển từ phòng ngự sang tấn công giúp anh chiếm ưu thế trong các loạt bóng bền, vốn là điểm mạnh của đối thủ người Đức.
Sau những game đầu giằng co, Alcaraz hai lần giành break để dẫn 4-1. Dù Zverev đòi lại một game giao bóng, tay vợt Đức tiếp tục mất bình tĩnh và để đối thủ bẻ giao bóng lần thứ ba trong set.
Sự tương phản thể hiện rõ qua ngôn ngữ cơ thể. Alcaraz mỉm cười sau pha lốp bóng qua hai chân khiến Zverev đánh hỏng cú smash trên lưới. Trong khi đó, tay vợt Đức ném vợt vì thất vọng và bị trọng tài nhắc nhở lần thứ hai về lỗi chậm thời gian.
Zverev chỉ ghi ba điểm winner nhưng mắc tới 19 lỗi tự đánh hỏng trong set đầu, trước khi thua 2-6. Đây là sự sa sút đáng kể với tay vợt đã dựa vào khả năng giao bóng ổn định để tiến đến chung kết mà không thua set nào.
Thế trận tưởng như tiếp tục nghiêng về Alcaraz khi anh giành break thứ tư trong trận ở set hai. Tuy nhiên, Zverev không dễ dàng đầu hàng. Tay vợt Đức cải thiện khả năng giao bóng và tận dụng thời điểm đối thủ chùng xuống để đòi lại break ở game thứ tám. Hai người sau đó giữ game giao bóng, đưa set đấu vào loạt tie-break.
Zverevbị dẫn 0-3 nhưng bất ngờ thắng liền sáu điểm, qua đó có ba set-point liên tiếp. Nếu tận dụng thành công, tay vợt Đức sẽ kéo trận đấu sang set quyết định và có cơ hội giành danh hiệu ATP Finals thứ ba.
Nhưng đúng thời điểm đối mặt nguy cơ mất set, Alcaraz thể hiện bản lĩnh. Anh cứu cả ba set-point, trong đó có một điểm khi Zverev cầm giao bóng, rồi đưa tỷ số về thế cân bằng. Tay vợt Tây Ban Nha sau đó tận dụng match-point thứ hai bằng cú trái tay ghi điểm winner, ấn định chiến thắng 9-7 trong loạt tie-break.
Zverev (trái) chúc mừng Alcaraz sau trận chung kết tại Turin, Italy, ngày 22/11/2026. Ảnh:Reuters
Điều đáng chú ý làAlcarazbước vào chung kết khi thể trạng chưa hoàn toàn bình phục. Anh vẫn phải quấn băng hỗ trợ phần trên đùi trái sau khi gặp vấn đề ở gân kheo trong tuần thi đấu tại Turin.
Ở bán kết, tay vợt Tây Ban Nha từng thừa nhận không thể di chuyển với cường độ cao nhất và phải hạn chế những pha đuổi bóng có nguy cơ khiến chấn thương nghiêm trọng hơn. Dù vậy, trước Zverev, anh vẫn duy trì tốc độ, khả năng phòng ngự và những cú đánh sáng tạo ở các thời điểm quyết định.
Chức vô địch ATP Finals đánh dấu chặng cuối của màn trở lại ấn tượng mà Alcaraz thực hiện chỉ trong 84 ngày kể từ khi tái xuất ở Mỹ Mở rộng. Với Zverev, tay vợt Đức kết thúc năm với 69 trận thắng, nhiều nhất ATP Tour, và vị trí số một thế giới. Hai danh hiệu Grand Slam đầu tiên cùng ngôi đầu bảng thứ bậc vẫn biến 2026 thành mùa giải thành công nhất sự nghiệp của anh.

Alcaraz puts Zverev in shade as world’s best beats No 1 for first ATP Finals title | ATP Finals | The GuardianSkip to main contentSkip to navigation
Carlos Alcaraz enjoys winning his first ATP Finals title of his career.Photograph: Luca Bruno/APView image in fullscreenCarlos Alcaraz enjoys winning his first ATP Finals title of his career.Photograph: Luca Bruno/AP
Alcaraz puts Zverev in shade as world’s best beats No 1 for first ATP Finals title
Spaniard wins final 6-2, 7-6 (7) against new world No 1
Alcaraz the fourth to win career grand slam and ATP Finals
The titles of ATP world No 1 and the best male tennis player in the world are carried by two different names. This has always been clear throughout this messy, injury-ravaged men’s season but it was underlined in the grand finale as Carlos Alcaraz ended his campaign with a statement victory, defeating the top-ranked player,Alexander Zverev, 6-2, 7-6 (7) to win the ATP Finals for the first time.
So much of Alcaraz’s fortunes this season were defined by the wrist injury that forced him out for four and a half months during the spring and summer. No matter, he still managed to tick the two most important items off his to-do list this year.
After starting 2026 by becoming the youngest man in history to earn the career grand slam, he is now, at 23, the fourth man to win all four grand slams and theATP Finals. Despite his long absence, he has missed only two of the four majors and two of the nine Masters 1000 events: the Canadian Open and Shanghai Masters.
Carlos Alcaraz beats Alexander Zverev to seal ATP Finals glory – as it happenedRead more
Faster indoor courts were previously viewed as the conditions that make Alcaraz most vulnerable. It is fair to say that this is no longer true. Alcaraz ends his year on a 14-match winning streak after triumphing on two of the fastest courts, Paris and Turin.
This victory is all the more impressive considering he picked up a thigh injury during his match on Wednesdayagainst Daniil Medvedev. Although he kept on winning, the Spaniard has been more cautious with his peerless movement and his leg has been heavily taped. He has learned that he does not always need to throw himself around the court at 100% intensity, that he can actually conserve energy, play more efficiently and still defeat the best players in the world. That might just be the most worrying development for the rest of the field.
Until the final, Zverev’s tournament had served as another demonstration of his enormous yet freakishly consistent serve, with the German not dropping serve at all en oute to the final. However, the opening game immediately underscored how much better Alcaraz is than the rest of the top 10.
The Spaniard immediately generated three break points on Zverev’s serve. In Zverev’s second service game, Alcaraz landed ample returns, forced Zverev into baseline exchanges and broke to love.
View image in fullscreenWorld No 1 Alexander Zverev was unable to match the level of Carlos Alcaraz in the final.Photograph: Luca Bruno/AP
For much of the match, Alcaraz completely outplayed Zverev from the baseline. His concerns surrounding his thigh problems have forced him to play even more offensively as usual, and he has struck the ball so sweetly for most of the tournament, but he was also incredibly smart. He peppered Zverev with ample slices and slower balls, drawing short balls from the German by arresting his rhythm, before unleashing in full. Alcaraz’s forehand, the best in the world, usually commands all the attention, but he struck his backhand incredibly well all match.
However, even for a player who has won so much at such a young age, he rarely makes things easy for himself. From 6-2, 4-2, Alcaraz began to spray unforced errors as he fell to 4-5, 0-30 on his serve in set two. Then, after recovering to lead 3-0 in the tie‑break, Alcaraz suddenly trailed by triple set point at 3-6.
During this stretch, Zverev served well, he forced the Spaniard to earn every point through his consistent defence and came up with improvisational solutions to Alcaraz’s drop shots and variation on some decisive moments. The Spaniard, however, was extremely poor.
Things may not often be straightforward for Alcaraz: his ability to play his best tennis when it most matters remains an astounding quality. To the surprise of nobody at all, he locked in, saved the three set points, earned a match point with a sickly sweet point-ending drop shot and then, without hesitation, he pounded a backhand down-the-line winner to close out the victory.
After ample discourse surrounding his credibility as the new No 1, which Zverev complained about during the Paris Masters, he did respond in the right way on the court here, reaching the final with wins against four top 10 opponents.
But there are levels to this game and the gap between Alcaraz and the rest of the field in Turin this year is vast. He ends his individual season by providing an unforgettable reminder of the excellence the sport had to go without for so long.
